Chapter Two. The Lighthouse Keeper's Ledger

Marta Quiroga arrived at the lighthouse on Isla Brava in the autumn of 1931, carrying a trunk of books and a letter of appointment from the maritime authority. The previous keeper, an old man named Tobías, had left three weeks earlier, and the lamp had been tended in the meantime by a fisherman from the village who could not read.

On her first night she found the keeper's ledger on the table beneath the lamp room. Every entry recorded the hour the lamp was lit, the hour it was extinguished, the weather, and the ships that passed. Tobías had written in a small, careful hand for twenty-two years. The fisherman had added nothing but crosses.

Marta read the ledger backwards, from the last entry to the first, during the storms of that winter. She discovered that Tobías had noted a light moving along the northern cliffs on eleven nights, always in the month of March, and always when the sea was calm. He had never explained it.

In March of 1932 Marta saw the light herself. It was a lantern carried by a boy from the village, who walked the cliff path to meet a smuggler's boat. When she confronted the boy's father, the fisherman who had tended the lamp, he confessed that the smugglers paid the village to keep the lighthouse dark on those nights, and that Tobías had refused for twenty years.

Marta kept the lamp lit every night that March. At the end of the month she wrote a single sentence in the ledger: the light on the cliffs had stopped.
